title: Bengaluru Startup Akashalabdhi Tests Inflatable Space Habitat in Balloon Flight
excerpt: Project Indra, an expandable habitat built for a crew of three, completed a balloon-borne test over Adampur, Punjab — a first step towards habitats for future space missions.
body:
• Bengaluru spacetech startup Akashalabdhi has completed a balloon-borne test of its inflatable space habitat, Project Indra, over Adampur in Punjab.
  • The habitat is an expandable structure designed for a crew of three, with radiation shielding, micrometeorite protection and thermal insulation.
  • The test, on October 29–30, took the structure to about 75 metres for roughly six minutes at peak altitude.
  • Next steps in 2027: a paraglider drop test and a scale model. Business Standard reports the space-segments market is expected to reach US$5.1 billion by 2040.

A Bengaluru startup has taken an early step towards building homes for astronauts. Akashalabdhi, a spacetech company launched in October 2024 by a former Indian Army officer, has completed what it describes as a first-of-its-kind test in India: a balloon-borne flight of an inflatable habitat module designed for future space missions, according to India Today.

What was tested

The structure, named Project Indra, is an expandable habitat engineered for a crew of three. It is designed to provide radiation shielding, protection against micrometeorites and thermal insulation — the three problems any long-duration habitat must solve. In the test, carried out on October 29–30 from Adampur in Punjab, the module was carried aloft by balloon to about 75 metres and held at peak altitude for roughly six minutes, validating the basic structure before more demanding trials.

"The successful test is an important step, not just for us, but for India."

— S.M. Vaidya, chairman, speaking at the company's launch

Why inflatable habitats

Inflatable — or expandable — modules are attractive for one simple reason: launch volume. A habitat that can be packed small and expanded in orbit gives astronauts far more living and working space than a rigid module of the same launch size, which is why space agencies and private firms abroad have pursued the concept for space stations and, eventually, surface habitats on the Moon and Mars. Akashalabdhi is positioning Project Indra in that market; Business Standard reports the space-segments market is expected to reach US$5.1 billion by 2040.

What comes next

The balloon flight is the first rung of the test ladder, not the last. The company's stated roadmap for 2027 includes a paraglider drop test of the structure and the development of a scale model — steps towards proving the habitat can survive deployment and descent loads before any orbital demonstration. The startup, launched in October 2024 by a former Indian Army officer, is part of a growing cohort of Indian private spacetech firms moving beyond rockets and satellites into the infrastructure astronauts will live in.
nri_angle: An Indian private spacetech firm entering the space-habitat segment long dominated by US and European players.
